newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti calm despite violence threats around strike.
newsitem.headline: Haiti calm despite violence threats around strike.

text.p: A general strike closed schools and hobbled business in Haiti on Thursday but police claimed victory in keeping the peace despite threats of violence by militant organisers.
Sporadic rock-throwing incidents were reported in the capital and United Nations workers were airlifted from Cap-Haitien because of unrest there on Wednesday.
The call by militant government opponents for a general strike was heeded as street merchants stayed home, car and pedestrian traffic was sparse and schools and many businesses were shut tight.

Yet despite a warning from organisers that the streets would "run with red, red, red" if the strike call was ignored, government offices were open, some businesses reopened in early afternoon and people began to appear in public when it became apparent that calm prevailed.
"The police have kept the peace and the population has largely felt comfortable to go ahead with their day," Haitian National Police spokesman Felder Jean-Baptiste said.

The strike was the latest in a series of protests by popular organisations calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Rosny Smarth and a change in the country's economic plan, in which nine state-run enterprises will be privatised.

Smarth's office issued a statement congratulating Haitians and the police for maintaining calm. "The majority of citizens continued their activities as is their right," the statement said. "The government reaffirms its will to guarantee order and to prevent any attempt to destabilise the democratic institutions in the country."

Cite Soleil, the largest of Port-au-Prince's slums where violence often erupts, was also calm. Burning tires and barricades, often set up by protesters to show discontent, were not seen, but a small group of protesters threw rocks and smashed the windscreens of cars driving through the Port-au-Prince suburb of Delmas.
"It was a gamble to go out," one of the few taxi drivers working said. "I need money, but a new windscreen is expensive, too."

In the northern city of Cap-Haitien, where the strike began on Wednesday, barricades were still in place. At least three people were wounded in a clash between police and protesters on Wednesday, but the mood was more relaxed on Thursday, according to U.N. sources.
The office of the United Nations Civilian Mission was closed and 10 workers were flown out of the city.
President Rene Preval has continued to support Smarth, and Smarth has said he will not resign unless asked to by Preval. Preval has said he would not give in to the organisations' demands.

The organisations called the strike "Operation Koupe Tet, Boule Kay," Creole words for "Cutting Heads and Burning Houses" after the rallying cry of Haiti's bloody 1803 slave revolt. The general strike was the second in two months.
The capital has been rocked by gang violence in recent days. At least 19 people have been killed, including three police officers, according to the United Nations.
